question: What is the state of their eyes?

positions.position: Their gaze is downcast, humbled and unable to lift in shame or fear.
positions.reasons: Muqātil and al-Wāḥidī link it to seeing the Fire and becoming sure of punishment; al-Jishumī adds fearful expectation; al-Kāshifī describes bowed heads; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a transfer from the posture of an abased person. Al-Biqāʿī says the eyes show the heart.

positions.position: Their eyes are humbled and confused because the luminous faculty is lost.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī says they cannot look into the world of light or perceive its joyful radiance.

turns_on: Whether the description is outward abasement or an inward loss of perception.

question: Why is humility assigned to the eyes?

positions.position: The eyes visibly reveal the humility of the whole person.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Samīn say all limbs are humbled; Bursawī says the heart is its source; al-Jishumī and al-Biqāʿī say the eyes show the inner condition.

question: How is خَٰشِعَةً أَبْصَٰرُهُمْ constructed?

positions.position: خَٰشِعَةً is an accusative circumstantial qualifier, and أبصارهم is its nominative subject.
positions.reasons: Al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī attach the circumstance to their inability in 68:42; al-Nasafī, al-Samīn, Bursawī, and al-Ālūsī relate it to those summoned. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī counts it as the first of two circumstances.

positions.position: Both words may be nominative as subject and predicate.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās gives this as an alternative to the accusative analysis.

turns_on: Whether خاشعة is read as a circumstantial accusative or with أبصارهم as a nominal sentence.

question: What does تَرْهَقُهُمْ mean?

positions.position: It reaches, covers, overtakes or overwhelms them.
positions.reasons: Bursawī explains rahq as one thing covering another; Ibn ʿĀshūr adds eager approach and compares 80:41. Al-Biqāʿī says the shame overpowers them.

question: What is the humiliation that overtakes them?

positions.position: It is severe, visible disgrace and abasement.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī says their submission becomes visible; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the soul's humiliation appears externally; Bursawī derives it from the root and dhalīl; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses that it is coercive.

positions.position: It is the shame of regret and grief at their refusal and inability.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies remorse; al-Rāzī likens them to a servant abandoned and shamed by his master; al-Biqāʿī traces shame to limbs spent on pleasures away from God; Ibn Kathīr calls it reversal of worldly arrogance.

positions.position: It comes from God's punishment when they see the Fire.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī names divine punishment; Muqātil and al-Wāḥidī say their eyes lower on seeing the Fire or certainty of punishment.

positions.position: It is inward attachment to lower things and bodily nature.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī describes stagnation in inferior passive states.

turns_on: Whether the disgrace is described as outward shame, remorse, punishment, or inward attachment.

question: How is تَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌۭ related syntactically to the preceding description?

positions.position: It is a second circumstantial clause describing those unable or summoned.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās allows an accusative circumstantial clause; Ibn ʿĀshūr attaches it to the pronoun in 'they are unable'; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī counts two circumstantial clauses.

positions.position: It can be detached from the preceding clause.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās gives this alternative.

turns_on: Whether the clause is circumstantial or independent.

question: What happens to believers' and nonbelievers' faces after the prostration?

positions.position: Believers' faces shine white or bright; hypocrites' and disbelievers' faces blacken.
positions.reasons: Al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī say whiter than snow and darker than pitch; al-Biqāʿī says brighter than the sun; Abū al-Layth includes Jews and Christians among those grieving with dark faces.

question: Whom does the failed prostration expose?

positions.position: It exposes hypocrites who stood among Muslims.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly prefers the allusion to hypocrites; reports repeatedly contrast true believers with hypocrites whose backs stiffen. Al-Qurṭubī says this report pattern is established in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim through Abū Saʿīd and others.

positions.position: It also includes unbelievers or polytheists who rejected God's summons.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās names unbelievers; Ibn Kathīr and the Turkish commentary name both disbelievers and hypocrites; al-Shawkānī's narration says even unbelievers wish to prostrate.

positions.position: It includes people whose worldly prostrations were ostentatious or fearful.
positions.reasons: Abū Saʿīd's Prophetic report contrasts willing, sincere prostration with fear or display; the Turkish commentary reports the ostentatious men and women cannot bend.

turns_on: Whether the failed test is aimed at hidden hypocrisy, open disbelief, or insincere worship.

question: What scene unfolds when people are summoned to prostrate on Judgment Day?

positions.position: True worshippers recognize God at the disclosure and prostrate; hypocrites try but cannot.
positions.reasons: Abū Saʿīd, Abū Hurayra, Ibn Masʿūd, Qatāda, and other transmitted accounts give the shared contrast; backs become rigid, flat, fused, or one bone. Al-Qurṭubī says its meaning occurs in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim; al-Dāraquṭnī and al-Ḥākim grade the Ibn Masʿūd account sound.

positions.position: After forty years of standing, worshippers follow false gods to Hell; sincere Muslims prostrate and hypocrites are sent to Hell.
positions.reasons: Ibn Masʿūd and ʿAbdallāh report the forty years; al-Ṭabarī's accounts mention believers then enter Paradise and receive rewards; al-Thaʿlabī's version says the gathering is barefoot and naked; al-Qurṭubī's version includes a declaration of divine justice and compares 83:6.

positions.position: After other worshippers are led away, believers recognize God by a sign; hypocrites fall backward, and survivors cross a bridge by varying lights.
positions.reasons: Abū Hurayra names angels resembling ʿUzayr and Jesus and a prior settling of wrongs; his other report describes bridge speeds. Ibn Masʿūd's report says light varies by deeds and may flicker at the feet.

positions.position: Idol worshippers, Jews and Christians are separated before the remaining worshippers meet their Lord.
positions.reasons: Abū Saʿīd's accounts say other groups follow their objects of worship; one al-Ṭabarī transmission merely recalls the coming described before; al-Ḥasan's report says Muslims remain to be tested.

positions.position: In Abū Mūsā's account, monotheists recognize the Lord when the veil lifts, and each is replaced by a Jew or Christian in Hell.
positions.reasons: Abū Bardah swore three times his father transmitted it; ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz liked no report about monotheists more. Al-Qurṭubī states no grading there.

positions.position: Qatāda's account describes the unveiling as a horrendous event in which believers' prostration rebukes hypocrites.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī also transmits a Prophetic form of the report; the specific stress is humiliation brought by believers' act.

turns_on: The reports vary in sequence, forty-year duration, accompanying signs, final destinations and named groups.

question: Why can some people not prostrate then?

positions.position: Their backs or bodies are made rigid, fused or jointless, so they cannot bend.
positions.reasons: Ibn Masʿūd says one bone without joints; Muqātil likens backs to iron spits; other reports say flat or joined spines and falling backward. Al-Rāzī says God removes their capacity to heighten regret.

positions.position: The period of worship and obligation has ended, making the missed opportunity irreversible.
positions.reasons: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects accounts of lost joints, fused vertebrae, and rigidity after forty years as contrary to the text and context; she compares the belated wish in 89:23–25.

positions.position: Their souls have lost the capacity to answer truth because of afflictions acquired after worldly life.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī gives this as one account of what their former safety lacked.

turns_on: Whether inability is bodily, the close of the time for worship, or a lost spiritual capacity.

question: Why are they called to prostrate on that Day?

positions.position: The call tests and distinguishes sincere believers from hypocrites.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr says it honors the former and exposes the latter; Qatāda says believers' act humiliates hypocrites; al-Ḥasan says Muslims remain for testing.

positions.position: The call rebukes their earlier refusal and increases regret; it is no new legal duty.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī, Elmalılı and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ emphasize rebuke; Elmalılı rejects Abū Muslim's claim Resurrection is impossible for a summons because rebuke requires no legal command. Islahi says the summons exposes their lack of excuse.

positions.position: The summons gives sincere worshippers permission to prostrate.
positions.reasons: The Prophetic report via Qatāda and Qatāda's own account say believers are allowed to prostrate; the rest cannot.

turns_on: Whether the scene is framed chiefly as test, rebuke, or permission for true worshippers.

question: When was the earlier summons to prostrate?

positions.position: It was during worldly life, when response was possible.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī explicitly says both the summons and safety refer to worldly life; Ibn ʿAbbās contrasts former security with present fear. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the clause parenthetic recollection. Al-Qushayrī says recalling the old call makes proof decisive and regret sharper.

positions.position: The warning may also meet them at the end of life or beginning of the next.
positions.reasons: Al-Qushayrī leaves both boundaries possible. Abū Muslim proposes the last day of a life, when angels bring no good news and late conversion fails, with 25:22 and 6:158; another explanation has a dying patient unable to rise.

positions.position: It can describe illness, old age or incapacity while still in this life.
positions.reasons: Abū Muslim proposes bodily incapacity following prior soundness; Elmalılı permits this worldly reading but rejects exclusion of Resurrection.

turns_on: Whether the warning's immediate scene is Resurrection, life's end, or worldly incapacity.

question: What does the earlier call to prostrate ask of them?

positions.position: It asks for the prescribed ritual prayers, represented by their prostration.
positions.reasons: Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, al-Shaʿbī, al-Nakhaʿī and Qatāda identify obligatory prayer; some specify all five. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr identifies the summons to congregational prayer. Bursawī says prayer contains prostrations. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī dismisses this reading.

positions.position: It asks for literal prostration to God and worship of Him.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī says no impediment then; the call was freely rejected despite ability. Some accounts make worldly sincere prostration the condition for prostration on Judgment Day.

positions.position: Prostration stands for all acts of obedience or the summons of religious obligation.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports some interpreters: prostration is greatest obedience and the later test. Al-Qurṭubī says the explanations are close; al-Ālūsī gives the wider obligation reading; Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbdallāh speak of obeying commands and avoiding prohibitions.

positions.position: It means inward surrender and readiness to receive the world of light.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī says their faculties and readiness were still present, allowing future happiness.

positions.position: It summons people to worship God alone in submission to His lordship.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr says the parenthesis recalls this; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links afterlife felicity to worldly acknowledgment of God's sole lordship.

turns_on: Whether sujūd denotes bodily prostration, prayer, all obedience, or inward surrender.

question: How was the earlier summons delivered?

positions.position: Through the adhān and iqāma, especially 'Come to success' or 'Come to prayer'.
positions.reasons: Ibrāhīm al-Taymī names adhān and iqāma; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says they heard 'Come to success' yet did not come; Ibn ʿAbbās gives hearing and ignoring the call; Bursawī also cites scholars' invitations.

positions.position: Through God's command, the Prophet, prophets, religious teachers, or the imposed religious duty.
positions.reasons: Bursawī reports divine commands to establish prayer and Prophetic invitation; the Prophet's instruction to pray five times, fast, give zakāt and obey promised Paradise. He cites the report that a servant is nearest God in prostration; al-Nasafī says prophets called; al-Biqāʿī says callers to God.

positions.position: By a caller who invites prostration on Resurrection Day.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid and Qatāda describe that caller; the summons publicly exposes hypocrites.

turns_on: Whether the wording points to the public prayer call, wider divine and prophetic commands, or the afterlife caller.

question: What does سَٰلِمُونَ mean here?

positions.position: They were healthy, physically sound and able, without impediment to prostration.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī says no obstacle; Ibn ʿAṭiyya contrasts their then flexible backs with later fused vertebrae; al-Biqāʿī says arrogance rather than weakness stopped them; Ibn ʿĀshūr defines salāma as absence of defects and disease. Elmalılı stresses safety and freedom.

positions.position: They were free from fear, unlike the fearful summons now.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās explicitly contrasts worldly security with present fear; al-Ṭabarī's link to 11:20 describes their inability to heed in both lives.

positions.position: Their faculties and readiness for inward felicity were intact.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī says they were able to receive the influx of the world of light and gain happiness.

positions.position: They were free of the afflictions that later destroyed the soul's capacity to answer truth.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī offers this before the simpler physical-ability interpretation.

turns_on: Whether safety refers to bodily health, freedom from fear, or inward capacity.

question: What is the grammar of وَهُمْ سَٰلِمُونَ?

positions.position: It is a waw-marked circumstantial clause describing those summoned in worldly life.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn gives its subject as the subject of the second yudʿawn; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the waw marks the circumstance.

question: What warning about congregational prayer is drawn from the verse?

positions.position: The verse warns those who hear the congregational prayer call but fail to attend.
positions.reasons: Kaʿb swears that it was revealed specifically about absentees; al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī and Ibn al-Jawzī apply the warning. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym came despite paralysis, urging even crawling; Ibn al-Musayyib answered despite a threat from Ṭāriq. Al-Qurṭubī points to his earlier discussion of congregational prayer's obligation.

positions.position: The verse concerns the five obligatory prayers when their call is made.
positions.reasons: Kaʿb's version in al-Durr names five prayers; other authorities identify prescribed prayer and its call.

turns_on: Whether the warning targets attendance at congregation specifically or neglect of prescribed prayer generally.

question: Why repeat the summons to prostrate explicitly?

positions.position: The explicit wording in place of a pronoun emphasizes the earlier summons.
positions.reasons: Bursawī also allows that the wording marks prostration as standing for prayer and its prostrations; al-Ālūsī agrees on emphasis.

question: Why single out prostration?

positions.position: It is the greatest act of obedience and serves as the decisive afterlife test.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes the figurative reading to some interpreters; Bursawī states the ranking directly. A Prophetic report cited by Bursawī says the servant is closest to the Lord while prostrating.

question: What unspoken response follows the earlier summons?

positions.position: Their refusal to answer is omitted because the context makes it evident.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī states the ellipsis; many explanations explicitly say they refused though capable.

question: How do the two verses pair ability and inability?

positions.position: The passage uses iḥtibāk: present inability implies omitted former ability, and former safety implies omitted present unsafety.
positions.reasons: Al-Biqāʿī states both halves of the correspondence.

question: What moral reversal does their condition teach?

positions.position: Their former arrogance and refusal return as helplessness, shame and regret.
positions.reasons: Ibn Kathīr calls it punishment opposite to worldly crimes; Elmalılı says they thought sinners wiser than believers and now desire what they refused; Islahi says their own bodies testify to lack of excuse; Study Quran says some Arabs deemed prostration humiliating but meet greater humiliation. Al-Ṭabarī invokes 11:20 for inability in both lives.

positions.position: The disclosure brings joy and honor to Muslims but dread and humiliation to criminals.
positions.reasons: Elmalılı stresses this opposed experience; the face-color reports portray the same reversal.

question: What links this scene to other verses?

positions.position: 11:20 parallels their failure to hear or see in life and to prostrate now.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿAbbās explicitly draw the link.

positions.position: 70:43–44 parallels emergence from graves with downcast eyes and ignominy.
positions.reasons: Islahi says the parallel clarifies the exposed-shin Day as severe upheaval; Muqātil connects lowered eyes on seeing the Fire to al-Qalam.

positions.position: 89:23–25 parallels the sinner's useless late wish to have prepared for true life.
positions.reasons: Bint al-Shāṭiʾ connects that wish to the missed time for prostration.

positions.position: 83:6 is invoked for the long standing before God.
positions.reasons: The report to ʿUmar names forty years of standing.

turns_on: The notes offer different scriptural parallels for the scene.

question: How does this passage fit its surrounding argument?

positions.position: It interrupts the argument about alleged partners to show that only worldly submission to God's sole lordship yields afterlife happiness.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the alleged partners cannot provide felicity or intercession at Resurrection.

positions.position: It depicts a cataclysmic Day that overturns dreams of worldly luxury.
positions.reasons: Islahi places the refusal to prostrate within that reversal and reads 70:43–44 as its parallel.

turns_on: The sources emphasize different surrounding themes.

question: What accounts for the Qur'an's inimitable expression?

positions.position: Its eloquent wording, exact placement, sound meanings and ordered joining of diverse excellences exceed human capacity.
positions.reasons: Al-Khaṭṭābī says substitution damages meaning or style; al-Burhān and al-Itqān enumerate doctrine, worship, law, ethics, exhortation, past and future reports, and proof joined to conclusion. They say only divine knowledge unites these qualities.

question: How did opponents characterize the Qur'an despite its effect on them?

positions.position: They called it poetry, sorcery or dictated ancient legends while acknowledging its sweetness.
positions.reasons: Al-Khaṭṭābī and later compilations say poetry was inferred from order and sorcery from inability to match it; the dictated-lore charge conflicted with knowledge that Muhammad was unlettered and had no nearby dictation helper, compared with 25:5.

question: What does the report about al-Walīd's deliberation say?

positions.position: After reflection, al-Walīd called the Qur'an human speech or sorcery.
positions.reasons: Al-Khaṭṭābī tentatively identifies him; the Qur'an recounts his thought and claims in 74:18, 74:24–25. Al-Burhān says frustration and stubbornness drove the claim.

question: Why do near-synonyms matter in Qur'anic wording?

positions.position: Words that overlap retain distinct meanings, so their exact placement matters.
positions.reasons: Al-Khaṭṭābī lists knowledge/recognition, praise/gratitude, and stinginess/miserliness; he says maʿrifa takes one object, ʿilm two, and one says 'recognize God' but 'know God' with an attribute such as just or powerful.

question: How did the practice of combining readings in one completion develop?

positions.position: Early readers completed one transmission at a time; combining readings in one completion became established later.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jazarī says earlier authorities largely omitted the topic; al-Ṣafrawī only hinted at it. He attributes omission to intensive repeated study: al-Ḥuṣrī reportedly made ninety completions over ten years, al-Kattānī was kept with ʿĀṣim by Ibn Mujāhid, and al-Wāsiṭī spent years on multiple completions. Some imams disliked combination as novel, but it became accepted.
